original_question: Prove or disprove that for every near-optimal planar n-point set P and every epsilon > 0, every constant-degree algebraic curve contains at most O(n^(0.5+epsilon)) points of P.
target_in_paper: Section 2, Problem 4 of the current arXiv version of 1406.1949 (the same question appears as Problem 5 on page 3 of the June 7, 2014 PDF draft): the open problem on whether near-optimal planar point sets can have a constant-degree curve containing as many as n^{1/2+epsilon} points.
correct_elements: Your draft is aimed at the right open problem: the Section 2 structural question about near-optimal planar point sets and heavy constant-degree curves. It correctly keeps the setting planar, uses near-optimal point sets rather than arbitrary sets, and preserves the paper's conjectural threshold n^{1/2+epsilon}. Your phrasing with an upper bound on |P ∩ C| is also mathematically equivalent in spirit to the paper's official 'no curve contains Omega(...) points' formulation.
missing_details: The draft does not define 'near-optimal'. In the paper, this means a set P of n points in R^2 with D(P)=O(n/sqrt(log n)), where D(P) is the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by pairs of points of P (Section 2, p. 2 of the June 7, 2014 PDF draft).
The ambient setting should be explicit: P is a finite subset of R^2 and n=|P|.

The paper's quantifier on epsilon is weaker than your draft: it asks for a sufficiently small positive constant epsilon, not for every epsilon > 0 (Section 2, Problem 4 in the current version / Problem 5 in the June 7, 2014 draft, p. 3).

To be fully stand-alone, 'constant-degree curve' should be defined as an algebraic curve C={(x,y) in R^2 : f(x,y)=0} for some polynomial f in R[x,y] whose total degree is bounded by an absolute constant independent of n (Section 3, paragraph before Problem 5 in the current version).

It should be made explicit that lines and circles are included in the final open problem; they are not excluded here, even though one intermediate bound quoted just before the problem applies only to curves with no line or circle components (Section 2, p. 3 of the June 7, 2014 PDF draft).
If O(.) or Omega(.) notation is used, the intended meaning is asymptotic in n; the hidden constants may depend on epsilon and on the fixed degree bound, but not on n.
There are no extra hypotheses here such as homogeneity, irreducibility, nilpotency, or positive-characteristic assumptions; adding any of those would broaden or distort the paper's scope.
refined_question: Let P be a set of n points in R^2, and let D(P) denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by pairs of points of P. Assume that P is near-optimal in the sense that D(P)=O(n/sqrt(log n)). Prove or disprove that, for a sufficiently small positive constant epsilon, no algebraic curve C subset R^2 defined by a polynomial in R[x,y] of total degree bounded by an absolute constant contains Omega(n^{1/2+epsilon}) points of P.
justification: This is the nearest official formulation to your draft. The draft is not asking for the Section 3 problem about the minimum number of distinct distances among points constrained to lie on a curve; instead, it asks about how many points of a near-optimal planar set can lie on a curve. That matches the Section 2 structural problem exactly. The surrounding Section 2 discussion first defines near-optimal sets, then records known bounds for lines, circles, and constant-degree algebraic curves, and finally poses the sharper open problem with exponent 1/2+epsilon. The only substantive ways in which your draft departs from the paper are that it omits the definition of near-optimality and strengthens the epsilon-quantifier from 'for sufficiently small epsilon > 0' to 'for every epsilon > 0'.
